facts.statement: The genus Latenivenatrix was described by van der Reest and Currie in 2017.
facts.quote: authority: van der Reest and Currie, 2017

facts.statement: The type specimen of Latenivenatrix was originally described in 1969 by Dale Alan Russell.
facts.quote: The type specimen, or holotype, of Latenivenatrix (CMN 12340) was originally described in 1969 by Dale Alan Russell

facts.statement: The holotype of Latenivenatrix was collected in 1968 by Irene Vanderloh from the Dinosaur Park Formation in Alberta, Canada.
facts.quote: It was collected in 1968 by Irene Vanderloh in the Dinosaur Park Formation strata from Alberta, Canada.

facts.statement: The name Latenivenatrix means "hiding huntress" and it is a genus of large troodontid dinosaur.
facts.quote: Latenivenatrix, meaning "hiding huntress", is a genus of large troodontid

facts.statement: Latenivenatrix is distinguished by a retroverted pubis forming a 17° angle and an anteriorly curved pubic shaft.
facts.quote: the pubis is retroverted forming a 17° angle; the pubic shaft is anteriorly curved

facts.statement: The frontal bones of Latenivenatrix are triangular in shape and feature a single deep groove on the frontonasal contact surface.
facts.quote: the triangular shape of each frontal bone which also does have a single deep groove in the frontonasal contact surface

facts.statement: Latenivenatrix possesses a concave anterior surface on metatarsal III.
facts.quote: a concave anterior surface of metatarsal III

facts.statement: The time range for Latenivenatrix is estimated to be between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: As a derived troodontid, Latenivenatrix was likely a semi-omnivorous biped that had lost the ability to fly.
facts.quote: As a derived troodontid, it was probably a semi-omnivorous biped with loss of the skills of a primitive flyer.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Latenivenatrix is a distinct genus or a junior synonym of Stenonychosaurus.
facts.quote: Although described as separate, it has been considered a junior synonym of Stenonychosaurus.

facts.statement: Some analyses have considered Latenivenatrix mcmasterae to be a junior synonym of Stenonychosaurus inequalis due to overlapping stratigraphic positions and lack of definitive diagnostic characters.
facts.quote: L. mcmasterae was considered to be a junior synonym of S. inequalis.

facts.statement: A parietal bone from Latenivenatrix bears a pathological aperture that may indicate injury or disease.
facts.quote: A parietal bone catalogued as TMP 79.8.1 bears a "pathological aperture".

facts.statement: Researchers have debated the cause of a pathological aperture in a Latenivenatrix parietal bone, with hypotheses ranging from a cyst to a bite wound.
facts.quote: In 1985, Phil Currie hypothesized that this aperture was caused by a cyst. Tanke and Rothschild interpreted it as a possible bite wound in 1999.

facts.statement: A hatchling specimen of Latenivenatrix shows evidence of a congenital defect causing a twisted jaw.
facts.quote: One hatchling specimen may have suffered from a congenital defect, which resulted in the front part of its jaw being twisted.

facts.statement: Latenivenatrix is classified as a derived troodontid within the subfamily Troodontinae, likely related to Asian contemporaries like Linhevenator and Philovenator.
facts.quote: Latenivenatrix was found to be a derived troodontid (part of the newly defined Troodontinae), probably related to coeval Asian forms such as Linhevenator and Philovenator.

facts.statement: A parietal bone catalogued as TMP 79.8.1 has a pathological aperture.
facts.quote: Un hueso parietal catalogado como TMP 79.8.1 tiene una "abertura patológica".

rejected.quote: With an estimated skull length of 45 cm and a full body length of 3 - 3.5 m, Latenivenatrix is the largest troodontid known.
